question: C major to C minor moves one note down by one key. Who hears that single step as sad?
answer: Mostly people raised on Western music. In Dalla Bella's tests, 3- and 4-year-olds could not tell happy music from sad, 5-year-olds went by tempo alone, and mode counted only from 6 to 8. In a Papua New Guinea valley with little Western music, minor cadences were not heard as sadder.
move: Before calling a reaction natural, ask when you first learned it.
ask: Which of my gut reactions did I actually learn as a child?

scene.hint: Tap keys to change the chord. Every tap plays it.

moments.name: Major chord
moments.text: Bright, to ears raised on pop and hymns. Now lower the E by one key, to Eb.

moments.name: Minor chord
moments.text: One note, one key lower. Sad? Under age 6, children mostly can't hear it.

moments.name: No third
moments.text: Take the middle note out: neither happy nor sad. The third sets the mood.

moments.name: Minor third
moments.text: The step that decides, on its own. To Western ears it already leans dark.

reference: Dalla Bella, Peretz, Rousseau & Gosselin, A developmental study of the affective value of tempo and mode in music, Cognition 80, B1-B10, 2001; Smit, Milne, Sarvasy & Dean, Emotional responses in Papua New Guinea show negligible evidence for a universal effect of major versus minor music, PLOS ONE 17: e0269597, 2022
